109	  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
110	
111	The \$1,870 million figure (excluding ABL) is the figure used in the Company\'s public filings and press releases.
112	
113	**Ad Hoc Group Composition:** The Ad Hoc Group consists of nine (9) institutional investors holding approximately \$742.6 million in aggregate principal amount of the first lien term loan, representing approximately 62.4% of the \$1,190 million outstanding principal. The three largest holders are:
114	
115	  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
116	  **Holder**                          **Principal Amount Held**
117	  ----------------------------------- -----------------------------------
118	  Hollcroft Capital Management LP     \$218.5 million
119	
120	  Garrison Creek Asset Partners LLC   \$167.2 million
121	
122	  Northvane Investment Group Inc.     \$112.8 million
123	
124	  Remaining 6 holders (aggregate)     \$244.1 million
125	
126	  **Total Ad Hoc Group Holdings**     **\$742.6 million**
127	  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
128	
129	An important threshold note: while the Ad Hoc Group\'s 62.4% of outstanding first lien term loan principal exceeds the two-thirds in amount (66.67%) threshold required under 11 U.S.C. § 1126(c) when measured only against the voting claims of consenting lenders, 62.4% does *not* constitute two-thirds of the entire first lien class. Acceptance of a plan under Section 1126(c) requires both (i) at least two-thirds in amount and (ii) more than one-half in number of the allowed claims of holders that actually vote. Accordingly, it is critically important that the RSA lock-up provisions are robust and that the deal team explore opportunities to expand the consenting group to the extent practical, in order to ensure that the voting threshold is met even if some non-consenting holders vote to reject the plan.
130	
131	**[III. Negotiating Priorities --- Red Lines (Non-Negotiable)]{.underline}**
132	
133	The positions set forth in this Section III are positions that the Company must not concede in the course of negotiations. If at any point Sternwick & Calloway, on behalf of the Ad Hoc Group, insists on crossing any of these lines, the deal team must immediately escalate the matter to Partner Vasquez, who will confer with the Company\'s board of directors (through CEO Margaret T. Holloway, with input from General Counsel Susan K. Pratt and CFO David R. Nakamura) before any concession is made. No team member is authorized to agree to or signal willingness to concede any red line item without this escalation process.
134	
135	**[A. Fiduciary Out Must Be Preserved Without Undue Restrictions]{.underline}**
136	
137	The Company\'s RSA draft provides that the Board of Directors may terminate the RSA if continued performance would be inconsistent with the directors\' fiduciary duties under applicable law, subject to five (5) business days\' advance written notice to the Ad Hoc Group. This fiduciary out provision is a **hard red line** and must be preserved substantially in its current form. The board\'s ability to exercise its fiduciary duties cannot be subject to conditions or restrictions that effectively prevent or impede the board from acting when circumstances require. Specifically:
138	
139	> **(a) Notice Period.** The notice period must remain at five (5) business days or shorter. Any extension beyond five business days creates unacceptable delay, particularly in a situation where a time-sensitive alternative transaction emerges and the counterparty to such transaction requires prompt certainty of commitment from the Company. A longer notice period effectively gives the Ad Hoc Group a blocking window during which they can marshal opposition to the alternative transaction or take other actions adverse to the Company\'s interests.
140	>
141	> **(b) No Disclosure of Alternative Transaction Details.** There must be no requirement that the Company disclose to the Ad Hoc Group the identity of any alternative transaction counterparty or the specific terms of any alternative proposal that triggered the board\'s fiduciary determination. Such a disclosure requirement would chill potential bidders --- many of whom will condition their proposals on strict confidentiality --- and would effectively provide the Ad Hoc Group with competitive intelligence to block or match the proposal without engaging in a genuine competitive process. Any information disclosed to the Ad Hoc Group would inevitably be shared among its nine constituent members, many of whom are active market participants who may hold positions in the Company\'s other debt tranches or in competing hospitality companies.
142	>
143	> **(c) No Break-Up Fee or Termination Fee.** The fiduciary out cannot be conditioned on the payment of a break-up fee, termination fee, expense reimbursement, or any other monetary penalty. We anticipate that the Ad Hoc Group, through Sternwick & Calloway, will seek such a fee as a condition of the RSA. This is not acceptable. A termination fee tied to the exercise of fiduciary duties effectively imposes a tax on the board\'s exercise of its legal obligations and creates a practical barrier to the consideration of superior alternatives.
144	
145	**Rationale:** Delaware law imposes fiduciary duties on the directors of Ridgeline Hospitality Group, Inc. that cannot be contractually waived or bargained away. An RSA that unduly restricts the board\'s ability to exercise those duties risks being unenforceable on public policy grounds and creates significant litigation exposure for the individual directors. Moreover, the United States Trustee and any official committee of unsecured creditors appointed in the Chapter 11 case will carefully scrutinize the fiduciary out provisions of the RSA. Overly restrictive terms could be cited as evidence that the RSA was coercive or that the Company\'s board did not independently and adequately consider alternatives --- arguments that could undermine confirmation.
146	
147	**Related Concern --- Alternative Transaction Provision.** The RSA draft provides the Ad Hoc Group with a ten (10) business day matching right and permits the Company to pursue an alternative transaction only if such transaction provides \"materially better\" recovery to stakeholders. The \"materially better\" standard is already protective of the Ad Hoc Group\'s interests, as it requires the Company to demonstrate a meaningful improvement over the Ad Hoc Group\'s deal, not merely a marginal one. We must resist any attempt by the Ad Hoc Group to (a) define \"materially better\" with a specific numerical threshold (e.g., a requirement that the alternative must provide at least a 10% or 15% improvement in aggregate recovery), as such a rigid threshold could prevent the board from pursuing transactions that are clearly superior on a holistic basis but happen to fall just below an arbitrary quantitative benchmark; or (b) extend the matching period beyond ten (10) business days, as extended matching periods chill bidder participation by creating uncertainty about whether the Company can execute a transaction in a timely manner. The ten-day matching period is already at the outer boundary of market practice for RSA alternative transaction provisions; anything longer would be viewed as a lockout mechanism rather than a legitimate matching right.
148	
149	**[B. DIP Economics Must Be Defensible at Approval Hearing]{.underline}**
150	
151	The Company\'s RSA draft proposes a \$175 million new money debtor-in-possession credit facility (the \"DIP Facility\") to be provided by certain members of the Ad Hoc Group, with the following economics:
152	
153	> • Interest Rate: SOFR + 650 basis points
154	>
155	> • Roll-Up: \$75 million of prepetition first lien term loan claims rolling into the exit facility (i.e., receiving super-priority administrative expense status and treatment pari passu with the DIP claims)
156	>
157	> • Maturity: 6 months from the petition date
158	
159	These terms represent the Company\'s opening position and reflect what Pendleton Hargrave & Co. (Allison W. Cheng) has advised is defensible at a DIP approval hearing before the Bankruptcy Court under 11 U.S.C. § 364. The DIP terms must withstand challenge from the U.S. Trustee and any official committee, both at the interim and final hearing stages.
160	
161	**Red lines on DIP economics are as follows:**
162	
163	> **(a) Interest Rate.** SOFR + 650 basis points is already at the high end of the market range for a company of Ridgeline\'s size, operational profile, and asset quality. Our analysis of comparable DIP facilities in the hospitality sector over the past eighteen months indicates a range of SOFR + 450 to SOFR + 700 basis points. We anticipate the Ad Hoc Group will push for higher pricing; any increase beyond SOFR + 700 basis points would be difficult to defend before the Court and the U.S. Trustee as consistent with the \"best interests\" standard. We should resist any rate above SOFR + 725 basis points at the absolute maximum. Even at SOFR + 725, we must be prepared to present Pendleton Hargrave\'s market analysis demonstrating that the rate is within the range of comparables, accounting for Ridgeline\'s specific risk profile.
164	>
165	> **(b) Roll-Up.** The \$75 million roll-up represents approximately 43% of the total \$175 million DIP commitment, which is a reasonable and defensible proportion. A full roll-up of the entire \$175 million DIP commitment would be highly problematic for several reasons: (i) it effectively converts all new money DIP claims into exit facility claims with super-priority status, materially diluting recoveries available to other creditor classes; (ii) a full roll-up will face vigorous challenge from any official committee of unsecured creditors and potentially from the U.S. Trustee, both of whom will argue that the roll-up is an impermissible value transfer; and (iii) in recent cases in the District of Delaware and the Southern District of Texas, courts have demonstrated increasing skepticism of full roll-ups, with several judges requesting detailed justification or reducing proposed roll-up amounts. We must hold the line at no more than \$100 million in roll-up (approximately 57% of the DIP commitment). Beyond \$100 million, the risk of an adverse ruling at the final DIP hearing increases materially.
166	>
167	> **(c) Fees.** The Company\'s RSA draft does not include upfront fees, commitment fees, or exit fees on the DIP Facility. If the Ad Hoc Group requests fees, we can accept a modest upfront fee of up to 1.5% (i.e., up to \$2.625 million on a \$175 million facility). However, we should resist exit fees entirely, as exit fees add to emergence costs and create a misaligned incentive structure (the DIP lenders benefit from a longer case). If exit fees are included, the combined DIP fees (upfront plus exit) must not exceed \$3 million in the aggregate.
168	>
169	> **(d) Total DIP Cost Budget.** When combining interest rate spread, fees, and the economic benefit of the roll-up amount, the total incremental cost of the DIP to the estate must remain at a level that can withstand a Section 364 challenge. Pendleton Hargrave has modeled that the Company\'s proposed terms (SOFR + 650, \$75M roll-up, no fees) result in total DIP cost (interest plus fees) of approximately \$17--18 million over a projected six-month case. We should resist any DIP package that pushes total cost (interest plus fees, exclusive of the roll-up economics) above \$22--23 million. Any package exceeding that threshold will invite sustained objection from junior creditor constituencies and heighten the risk of a contested DIP hearing.
170	
171	**[C. Professional Fee Carveout Must Be Adequate]{.underline}**
172	
173	The Company\'s RSA draft provides a professional fee carveout of \$15 million for Company professionals and \$7.5 million for Committee professionals, for an aggregate carveout of \$22.5 million. This is a **hard red line.** The \$22.5 million aggregate carveout reflects Ashford Pierce\'s estimate of the professional fees likely to be incurred in a prepackaged Chapter 11 case of this complexity and scope. Key factors justifying this amount include the following:
174	
175	> • Total funded debt of \$1.95 billion (including ABL) across four separate tranches, each with distinct collateral packages and priority structures
176	>
177	> • 214 hotel properties located across 31 states, requiring state-by-state regulatory, licensing, franchise agreement, and real property analysis
178	>
179	> • Approximately 11,400 employees with associated labor law, employee benefit, WARN Act, and COBRA compliance considerations
180	>
181	> • Multiple creditor constituencies --- ABL lender, first lien term loan lenders, second lien secured noteholders, unsecured noteholders, and trade creditors --- each likely to require separate professional engagement and analysis
182	>
183	> • Potential need for Greystone Whitaker LLP to serve as conflicts counsel for the Company on specific issues where Ashford Pierce may have a conflict
184	>
185	> • Hartfield & Dunn CPAs will need to perform audit, accounting, and tax advisory work in connection with the restructuring, including fresh-start accounting analysis
186	>
187	> • Pendleton Hargrave & Co. fees as the Company\'s financial advisor, including fees for plan valuation, feasibility analysis, and expert testimony
188	
189	The debtor professional carveout of \$15 million must not be reduced below \$12.5 million under any circumstances. The committee professional carveout of \$7.5 million must not be reduced below \$6 million. An inadequate professional fee carveout could (i) chill professional engagement if advisors perceive a material risk of not being fully compensated for their services, (ii) create a due process argument for creditor constituencies that they were denied adequate representation in the Chapter 11 case, and (iii) provide grounds for a motion to convert the case or appoint a Chapter 11 trustee if the debtor is unable to retain competent professionals. These are not theoretical concerns; in several recent cases, inadequate carveouts have led to significant delays, contested hearings, and in one instance, the conversion of a case from Chapter 11 to Chapter 7.
190	
191	If the Ad Hoc Group pushes back on the aggregate carveout amount, the deal team should emphasize that professional fees are a necessary and unavoidable cost of the restructuring process. Attempting to squeeze the professional fee carveout will be viewed unfavorably by the Court, which has an independent obligation to ensure that the debtor and creditor constituencies have adequate representation. A compressed carveout signals to the Court and to the U.S. Trustee that the DIP lenders are attempting to exert inappropriate control over the restructuring process by limiting the resources available to the estate and its creditors.
192	
193	**[D. Milestones Must Be Achievable]{.underline}**
194	
195	The Company\'s RSA draft proposes the following case milestones:
196	
197	  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
198	  **Milestone**                       **Deadline**
199	  ----------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------
200	  Chapter 11 Filing                   Within 5 business days of RSA effective date
201	
202	  Disclosure Statement Filed          Within 45 days of petition date
203	
204	  Disclosure Statement Approved       Within 90 days of petition date
205	
206	  Plan Confirmation                   Within 135 days of petition date
207	
208	  Emergence from Chapter 11           Within 165 days of petition date
209	  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
210	
211	These milestones are already aggressive for a case involving 214 hotel properties, \$1.95 billion in total funded debt, and multiple creditor constituencies, but they are achievable if the case proceeds on a substantially consensual track and the Bankruptcy Court\'s docket accommodates the proposed hearing schedule. The 45-day disclosure statement filing deadline, in particular, assumes that substantial preparation work on the disclosure statement, plan of reorganization, and solicitation materials will be completed before the petition date.
212	
213	**Red lines on milestones are as follows:**
214	
215	> **(a) Filing.** Five (5) business days from RSA execution is achievable because we will have substantially all first-day motions, declarations, and exhibits prepared before RSA execution. We should not accept anything shorter than three (3) business days. Even three days is tight --- the team will need time after RSA execution to finalize first-day declarations (incorporating the final RSA terms), update schedules, coordinate with the Company\'s treasury and accounting personnel, and prepare the petition and corporate authority documents. A filing deadline shorter than three business days introduces unnecessary execution risk that could result in a missed milestone on the first day of the RSA\'s life.
216	>
217	> **(b) Disclosure Statement Filing.** Forty-five (45) days is the minimum realistic timeline for preparing and filing a disclosure statement of the quality and completeness required in a case of this size. The disclosure statement must include a comprehensive description of the debtor\'s business, the proposed plan of reorganization, a liquidation analysis, projections, valuation analysis, risk factors, and applicable tax disclosures. If pressed, we could potentially agree to forty (40) days, but no shorter. Anything below forty days creates unacceptable execution risk and risks producing a disclosure statement that invites objections and delays.
218	>
219	> **(c) Disclosure Statement Approval.** Ninety (90) days provides a reasonable period for creditor review of the disclosure statement, the filing and resolution of any objections, and a hearing on the adequacy of the disclosure statement. If pressed, we could agree to eighty (80) days, but no shorter. This period must account for the possibility that the U.S. Trustee or a creditor constituency objects to the disclosure statement on the grounds of inadequate information, which would require revisions and potentially a supplemental hearing.
220	>
221	> **(d) Plan Confirmation.** One hundred thirty-five (135) days allows adequate time for solicitation of votes (typically 28--30 days), tabulation of ballots, resolution of any confirmation objections, and a confirmation hearing with testimony if required. If pressed, we could agree to as short as one hundred twenty (120) days, but no shorter. The solicitation period alone consumes nearly a month, and the tabulation and confirmation hearing preparation require additional time.
222	>
223	> **(e) Emergence.** One hundred sixty-five (165) days includes time for post-confirmation implementation steps, including obtaining necessary regulatory approvals (particularly state hotel licensing and franchise agreement transfers), closing mechanics for the exit financing, and the recording of relevant documents. If pressed, we could agree to one hundred fifty (150) days at the minimum, but no shorter.
224	
225	**Cure Periods for Missed Milestones.** The Company\'s RSA draft provides a ten (10) business day cure period for missed milestones. This cure period is essential and must be preserved. Missing a milestone may result from factors entirely outside the Company\'s control, including Bankruptcy Court scheduling constraints, unexpected creditor objections, or delays in the preparation and filing of third-party pleadings. We should not accept a cure period shorter than seven (7) business days.
226	
227	**Interaction with Termination Rights.** The deal team should bear in mind at all times that missed milestones are termination events under the RSA. If the milestones are unrealistically aggressive and the cure periods are shortened, the combined effect creates a de facto option for the Ad Hoc Group to exit the RSA on a pretext at any point during the case. This asymmetry of termination rights must be resisted. Milestones should be achievable with reasonable effort and good faith, not designed to function as hair-trigger termination mechanisms.
228	
229	**[E. Management Incentive Plan Must Be Sufficient to Retain Management]{.underline}**
230	
231	The Company\'s RSA draft reserves up to 10% of pro forma reorganized equity for a Management Incentive Plan (the \"MIP\"), with 50% of the MIP vesting upon emergence from Chapter 11 and the remaining 50% subject to time-based vesting over a three-year period following emergence.
232	
233	Margaret T. Holloway (CEO), David R. Nakamura (CFO), and the broader executive management team are critical to the Company\'s ongoing operations during the restructuring process and to value preservation and creation post-emergence. The Company operates 214 hotel properties across 31 states --- these assets cannot be managed effectively without experienced, industry-specific leadership. The loss of key management personnel during or immediately after the restructuring would materially impair the Company\'s enterprise value and could trigger operational disruptions that cascade across the portfolio, including potential franchise agreement defaults, guest experience degradation, and vendor payment disruptions.
234	
235	**Red lines on the MIP are as follows:**
236	
237	> **(a) MIP Size.** Ten percent (10%) of pro forma reorganized equity is the Company\'s target and is within the range of market practice, which typically falls between 8% and 12% in comparable hospitality restructurings based on Pendleton Hargrave\'s market survey. We should not accept a MIP below 8.5%. Below that level, we risk losing key members of the management team to competitors, which would materially impair the Company\'s value during a critical transition period. Several national hotel operators have been actively recruiting experienced restructuring-seasoned management teams, and the Company\'s executives have received and will continue to receive unsolicited outreach.
238	>
239	> **(b) Emergence Vesting.** At least 40% of the total MIP pool must vest upon emergence from Chapter 11. This provides management with immediate, tangible economic alignment with the reorganized entity from Day 1. Reducing emergence vesting below 40% undermines the retention incentive at the precise moment when management has the most attractive outside options. The period immediately following emergence is the highest-risk window for management departures, and the emergence vesting component is the primary retention mechanism during that window.
240	>
241	> **(c) Vesting Structure.** The balance of the MIP (after emergence vesting) should vest on a time-based schedule, not a performance-based schedule. Performance-based vesting introduces uncertainty that significantly reduces the perceived and actual retention value of the MIP awards. If the Ad Hoc Group insists on incorporating some performance component, we can accept a mixed structure --- for example, 50% of the non-emergence tranche vesting on a time basis and 50% vesting on a performance basis --- but we cannot accept a structure that is predominantly performance-based. Performance metrics in the hospitality industry are subject to significant macroeconomic variability (travel demand cycles, ADR and RevPAR fluctuations, seasonal patterns), and tying the majority of management\'s compensation to such metrics creates a misalignment between retention objectives and payout probability.
242	>
243	> **(d) Vesting Period.** The maximum vesting period for the non-emergence tranche must be three (3) years. Extending the vesting period beyond three years significantly diminishes the retention value of the MIP, especially for a management team that has already endured the stress, personal disruption, and reputational impact of a restructuring process. A four- or five-year vesting schedule effectively tells management that the economic benefit of the MIP is distant and contingent, which defeats the retention purpose.
244	
245	**Strategic Note.** The MIP negotiation is frequently used by secured lender groups to assert post-emergence control over management. The Ad Hoc Group\'s representatives on the reorganized board will have the authority to oversee management compensation going forward; however, the baseline MIP terms should be established and locked in the RSA itself, not left subject to post-emergence board discretion (which the Ad Hoc Group\'s board designees would effectively control). Leaving MIP terms to the post-emergence board creates a mechanism to coerce management compliance with lender preferences during the pendency of the Chapter 11 case, which is inappropriate and potentially actionable. The deal team should resist any effort to move the MIP from an RSA-specified term to a post-emergence governance matter.
246	
247	**[IV. Areas of Flexibility]{.underline}**
248	
249	The following positions represent areas where the Company has room to negotiate. These are **not** red lines. Concessions in these areas can be strategically offered in exchange for the Ad Hoc Group yielding on red line items described in Section III above. The deal team should manage these concessions carefully and avoid making multiple concessions simultaneously without securing reciprocal movement from the Ad Hoc Group.
250	
251	**[A. Equity Allocation]{.underline}**
252	
253	The Company\'s RSA draft proposes the following pre-MIP equity allocation:
254	
255	  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
256	  **Class**                           **Pro Forma Equity Allocation**
257	  ----------------------------------- -----------------------------------
258	  First Lien Term Loan                72%
259	
260	  Second Lien Secured Notes           12%
261	
262	  Senior Unsecured Notes              6%
263	
264	  **Subtotal (pre-MIP)**              **90%**
265	
266	  MIP Reserve                         10%
267	
268	  **Total**                           **100%**
269	  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
270	
271	**Flexibility:** The Company is willing to increase the first lien equity allocation up to 75% (from 72%), which would require a corresponding reduction to the second lien allocation (to 10%) and the unsecured allocation (to 5%), maintaining the 90% pre-MIP total (75% + 10% + 5% = 90%).
272	
273	**Limit:** We should not agree to a first lien equity allocation above 75%. Beyond 75%, the reductions to second lien and unsecured recoveries become so severe that obtaining consensual support from those classes becomes impractical. The second lien holders (represented by Kelton Harris & Roe LLP) have not yet been formally engaged in negotiations; offering them less than 10% of pro forma equity (down from an opening position of 12%) significantly increases the risk of a contested confirmation and cramdown litigation under 11 U.S.C. § 1129(b). Similarly, the unsecured noteholders (Atlas Fiduciary Services, Inc. as trustee) will in all likelihood organize their own ad hoc group if their projected recovery drops below 5%.
274	
275	**Strategic Note:** The equity allocation must be viewed holistically and in the context of the Company\'s overall plan strategy. The Company\'s plan depends on achieving consensual support from at least the first lien and second lien classes. Conceding too much equity to first lien at the expense of junior classes may produce a short-term agreement with the Ad Hoc Group but create a long-term confirmation problem that delays emergence and increases professional fees. Pendleton Hargrave (Allison Cheng) has advised that second lien notes are currently trading at approximately 28 cents on the dollar and unsecured notes at approximately 8 cents, which suggests that our proposed recoveries are in the range of current market expectations but are not overly generous for junior classes.
276	
277	**Total Equity Check:** Any equity allocation proposal must sum to exactly 90% pre-MIP (with 10% reserved for the MIP). The deal team should be vigilant about proposals from the Ad Hoc Group that reduce the MIP reserve and leave unallocated equity or that create separate pools (e.g., a \"rights offering equity pool\") that dilute the MIP or junior classes. Any ambiguity in the total equity allocation creates potential disputes that will consume time and resources during confirmation.
278	
279	**[B. Exit Term Loan Size]{.underline}**
280	
281	The Company\'s RSA draft proposes \$595 million in new first lien exit term loans, representing approximately 50% of the \$1,190 million face value of the existing first lien term loan.
282	
283	**Flexibility:** The Company can agree to an exit term loan of up to \$625 million (approximately 52.5% of the existing face value) if necessary to reach agreement on other terms. Pendleton Hargrave has advised that the reorganized Company\'s projected EBITDA and cash flow can service exit debt at this level, and the resulting leverage ratio would remain within the range of what the capital markets would consider sustainable for a hospitality company.
284	
285	**Limit:** The exit term loan should not exceed \$650 million. Beyond \$650 million, the reorganized Company\'s total leverage would exceed 3.5x projected EBITDA (\$187.3 million), which Pendleton Hargrave considers the upper boundary for a sustainable capital structure in the hospitality sector in the current macroeconomic environment. An over-leveraged emergence creates a material risk of financial distress recurring within a relatively short timeframe --- a so-called \"Chapter 22\" scenario --- which would be destructive to all stakeholders and to the Company\'s franchise and brand relationships.
286	
287	**[C. Governance / Board Composition]{.underline}**
288	
289	The Company\'s RSA draft does not specify post-emergence board composition in detail, leaving this as an item for negotiation.
290	
291	**Flexibility:** The Company is willing to discuss board composition for Reorganized Ridgeline Hospitality Group, Inc. Given that the first lien holders will receive a majority of the pro forma equity, it is reasonable and expected that they will seek proportionate board representation. We can accept a board structure in which the Ad Hoc Group designates a plurality or even a majority of the directors of the reorganized board, provided that (i) at least one (1) management designee (expected to be Margaret T. Holloway) is included, (ii) at least one to two (1--2) independent directors are included to satisfy governance best practices and potential listing standards, and (iii) standard corporate governance protections are maintained, including an independent audit committee and appropriate committee structures.
292	
293	**Limit:** The Company should not agree to any pre-petition governance concessions, such as board observer rights, lender consent rights over pre-petition operational decisions, or the appointment of a chief restructuring officer designated by the Ad Hoc Group prior to the bankruptcy filing. Pre-petition governance rights for creditors create significant legal risks, including potential equitable subordination claims, recharacterization arguments, and insider trading concerns arising from access to material non-public information. Such arrangements could complicate the Chapter 11 case and provide ammunition for challenges to the plan.
294	
295	**[D. Transfer Restrictions]{.underline}**
296	
297	The Company\'s RSA draft requires consenting lenders to transfer their first lien term loan positions only to other consenting lenders or to \"qualified transferees\" who agree to be bound by the RSA by executing a joinder within five (5) business days of the transfer.
298	
299	**Flexibility:** We can discuss extending the joinder period from five (5) business days to seven (7) business days if the Ad Hoc Group raises logistical concerns about the time required for a transferee to review the RSA and execute a joinder agreement. Seven business days is a reasonable accommodation that does not materially weaken the lock-up.
300	
301	**Limit:** We must resist any provision that allows transfers to non-consenting parties without a joinder requirement. The entire purpose of the RSA lock-up is to ensure that the requisite voting support for the plan is maintained throughout the pre-filing and post-filing periods. Any carve-out for transfers without joinder directly undermines the lock-up mechanism and creates a risk that locked-up support falls below the threshold necessary to confirm the plan by consent. Given that the Ad Hoc Group holds 62.4% of first lien claims, even modest leakage of claims to non-consenting holders could reduce aggregate support below the two-thirds in amount threshold required under Section 1126(c).
302	
303	**[V. Anticipated Counterparty Positions and Preemptive Strategy]{.underline}**
304	
305	Based on our preliminary discussions with Sternwick & Calloway, our review of Clearbridge Advisory\'s indicative term sheet, and our experience in similar restructuring negotiations in the hospitality sector, we anticipate the following positions from the Ad Hoc Group. The deal team should be prepared to address each of these points when we receive the markup.
306	
307	**[A. DIP Economics]{.underline}**
308	
309	The Ad Hoc Group will almost certainly push for higher pricing on the DIP Facility, likely in the range of SOFR + 750 to SOFR + 800 basis points. They will also likely request both an upfront fee (estimated 2.0%--3.0%) and an exit fee (estimated 1.0%--2.0%), as well as a full roll-up of the entire \$175 million DIP commitment into the exit facility. Our response should be to hold firm on the red lines described in Section III.B above and to use Pendleton Hargrave\'s market data on comparable DIP facilities (which Allison Cheng has been compiling) to demonstrate that our proposed terms are well within the market range and that the Ad Hoc Group\'s proposed terms exceed what courts have approved in recent cases. This establishes the baseline expectation for the DIP negotiation and positions us to make targeted, measured concessions within the ranges identified in Section III.B if necessary to close the deal.
310	
311	**[B. Milestones]{.underline}**
312	
313	The Ad Hoc Group will seek to compress the case milestones, particularly the disclosure statement filing deadline and the confirmation deadline. Jonathan Garvey\'s practice style tends toward aggressive case management timelines, and the Ad Hoc Group\'s members --- as holders of first lien debt --- are motivated to minimize the duration of the Chapter 11 case (which reduces administrative expense claims ahead of their distributions and limits the period during which market or operational conditions could deteriorate). Our response should be to push back with realistic timeline estimates supported by the deal team\'s preparation schedule, Ashford Pierce\'s assessment of Bankruptcy Court availability in the District of Delaware, and the observation that aggressive milestones paired with lender termination rights create perverse incentives for the Ad Hoc Group to terminate the RSA rather than work constructively through case complications.
314	
315	**[C. Cash Collateral / Operational Controls]{.underline}**
316	
317	The Ad Hoc Group may seek consent rights over the debtor\'s use of cash collateral during the Chapter 11 case, beyond the ordinary adequate protection provisions required under 11 U.S.C. § 363. While the first lien lenders are entitled to adequate protection of their security interests, any consent rights must be structured to avoid creating a de facto operational veto over the Company\'s business.
318	
319	Ridgeline operates 214 hotel properties across 31 states with approximately 11,400 employees. Routine operational expenditures --- including payroll, vendor payments, property maintenance and repair, seasonal capital expenditures (preparing for the summer travel season), franchise fees payable to brand franchisors, insurance premiums, real property taxes, and utility payments --- involve frequent transactions that can individually be significant in dollar amount. A single property renovation can cost several million dollars; seasonal staffing ramps across the portfolio can increase payroll costs by tens of millions of dollars in a given month. Any consent threshold for non-ordinary-course expenditures must be set at a level that accommodates these operational realities. We would suggest no lower than \$10 million per individual transaction and \$25 million in the aggregate for non-ordinary-course expenditures, with a corresponding budget that is updated monthly and subject to reasonable variance thresholds. Consent thresholds below these levels would paralyze the Company\'s day-to-day operations and force the Company to seek Ad Hoc Group approval for routine business decisions, which would be impractical, value-destructive, and would likely draw objection from the U.S. Trustee as an impermissible delegation of debtor-in-possession management authority to a creditor constituency.
320	
321	**[D. Releases]{.underline}**
322	
323	We anticipate that the Ad Hoc Group will seek broad releases as part of the plan of reorganization, potentially including third-party releases that would bind non-consenting parties. The Company\'s RSA draft currently includes mutual releases among the debtor, consenting lenders, and their respective professionals and advisors. Any expansion of the release framework should be evaluated carefully by the deal team, particularly in light of the evolving legal landscape around non-debtor, third-party releases following recent Supreme Court jurisprudence. The permissibility of such releases varies by circuit, and the deal team should consult with Ashford Pierce\'s appellate and Supreme Court practice group before committing to any specific release framework in the RSA.
324	
325	**[E. Liquidity Covenants / Termination Triggers]{.underline}**
326	
327	The Ad Hoc Group may seek to add a liquidity-based termination trigger to the RSA --- that is, a provision that permits the Ad Hoc Group to terminate the RSA if the Company\'s total liquidity falls below a specified floor. While the Company\'s current liquidity of approximately \$113 million provides a meaningful buffer, hotel operations are inherently seasonal and capital-intensive. The summer peak season (June through August) drives higher revenues but also substantially higher operating costs (increased staffing, higher utility consumption, accelerated maintenance). Any liquidity floor must account for these seasonal fluctuations and must be set at a level that does not give the Ad Hoc Group a hair-trigger termination right during a predictable low-liquidity period. If a liquidity floor is proposed, it should be measured on a trailing 30-day average basis (not a point-in-time test) and should not exceed \$30 million, which represents a reasonable distress threshold well below the Company\'s current liquidity position. We should resist the inclusion of a liquidity trigger entirely if possible, as the DIP Facility itself provides sufficient assurance of the Company\'s ability to fund operations through emergence.
328	
329	**[VI. Process and Coordination]{.underline}**
330	
331	The following instructions apply to all members of the deal team for the duration of the RSA negotiation process:
332	
333	1\. The RSA draft will be circulated to Sternwick & Calloway LLP (attention: Jonathan M. Garvey) on March 17, 2025. Ashford Pierce will transmit the draft with a brief cover letter identifying the document and proposing a schedule for initial feedback.
334	
335	2\. The deal team should expect to receive a markup from Sternwick & Calloway within approximately two (2) weeks of circulation, i.e., on or around March 31, 2025.
336	
337	3\. Upon receipt of the markup, the associate team (Sorensen, Chandrasekaran, and Whitfield) should prepare a comprehensive redline analysis memorandum for Partner Vasquez. The redline analysis should catalogue every material change, assess each change against the framework established in this memorandum (identifying whether the change affects a red line item, a flexibility item, or a new issue not previously addressed), and recommend a response for each change (accept, reject, or counter-propose with specific alternative language).
338	
339	4\. All communications with Sternwick & Calloway and Clearbridge Advisory must be coordinated through Partner Vasquez. No member of the deal team should convey substantive positions, signal areas of flexibility, or indicate willingness to concede on any point to opposing counsel or the Ad Hoc Group\'s financial advisor without prior approval from Partner Vasquez.
340	
341	5\. Pendleton Hargrave (Allison W. Cheng) should be consulted on all proposed changes to economic terms, including but not limited to DIP economics, exit facility terms, equity allocation, valuation-related provisions, and the MIP.
342	
343	6\. Susan K. Pratt (General Counsel) and the Ridgeline board of directors must approve any concession on red line items identified in Section III of this memorandum. Partner Vasquez will coordinate the approval process with Ms. Pratt and CEO Holloway directly.
344	
345	7\. The target RSA execution date of April 14, 2025 provides approximately four (4) weeks for negotiation from the date of RSA circulation. This is a tight timeline, particularly given the approaching debt maturities (ABL: June 15, 2025; senior unsecured notes: September 15, 2025). The deal team should be prepared for intensive, compressed rounds of negotiation and should maintain scheduling flexibility throughout the April 1--14 window.
346	
347	**[VII. Summary of Red Lines vs. Flexibility]{.underline}**
348	
349	The following table provides a quick-reference summary of all positions discussed in this memorandum:
350	
351	  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
352	  **Issue**                           **Company Position**             **Red Line (Non-Negotiable)**                      **Flexibility Range**
353	  ----------------------------------- -------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------- ------------------------
354	  Fiduciary Out Notice Period         5 business days                  Must not exceed 5 business days                    None
355	
356	  Fiduciary Out Disclosure Req.       None                             No disclosure of alternative transaction details   None
357	
358	  Alternative Transaction Standard    \"Materially better\" recovery   No specific numerical threshold                    None
359	
360	  Alternative Transaction Matching    10 business days                 No more than 10 business days                      None
361	
362	  DIP Interest Rate                   SOFR + 650 bps                   Must not exceed SOFR + 725 bps                     Up to SOFR + 725 bps
363	
364	  DIP Roll-Up                         \$75M                            Must not exceed \$100M                             Up to \$100M
365	
366	  DIP Fees                            None                             Combined fees ≤ \$3M                               Up to \$3M
367	
368	  Professional Carveout (Debtor)      \$15M                            Not below \$12.5M                                  Down to \$12.5M
369	
370	  Professional Carveout (Committee)   \$7.5M                           Not below \$6M                                     Down to \$6M
371	
372	  MIP Size                            10%                              Not below 8.5%                                     Down to 8.5%
373	
374	  MIP Emergence Vesting               50%                              Not below 40%                                      Down to 40%
375	
376	  MIP Vesting Type                    Time-based                       Not predominantly performance-based                Mixed acceptable
377	
378	  MIP Vesting Period                  3 years                          Not beyond 3 years                                 None
379	
380	  Filing Milestone                    5 business days                  Not less than 3 business days                      Down to 3 days
381	
382	  DS Filing Milestone                 45 days                          Not less than 40 days                              Down to 40 days
383	
384	  DS Approval Milestone               90 days                          Not less than 80 days                              Down to 80 days
385	
386	  Confirmation Milestone              135 days                         Not less than 120 days                             Down to 120 days
387	
388	  Emergence Milestone                 165 days                         Not less than 150 days                             Down to 150 days
389	
390	  Milestone Cure Period               10 business days                 Not less than 7 business days                      Down to 7 days
391	
392	  1L Equity Allocation                72%                              Not above 75%                                      Up to 75%
393	
394	  Exit Term Loan                      \$595M                           Not above \$650M                                   Up to \$625M
395	
396	  Transfer Joinder Period             5 business days                  Not more than 7 business days                      Up to 7 days
397	
398	  Transfer Without Joinder            Not permitted                    Must not be permitted                              None
399	
400	  Cash Collateral Consent             N/A                              Single txn ≥ \$10M / aggregate ≥ \$25M             See Section V.C
401	
402	  Liquidity Termination Trigger       Not proposed                     If included, ≤ \$30M trailing avg.                 Resist or cap at \$30M
403	
404	  Pre-Petition Board Observers        Not proposed                     Not acceptable                                     None
405	  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
406	
407	**[VIII. Conclusion]{.underline}**
408	
409	The overarching goal of the negotiations with the Ad Hoc Group is to execute a consensual Restructuring Support Agreement that locks up sufficient creditor support for a prepackaged Chapter 11 plan while simultaneously preserving (a) the Company\'s operational flexibility during the pendency of the Chapter 11 case, (b) the board of directors\' ability to exercise its fiduciary duties without undue restriction, and (c) adequate professional resources for the debtor and creditor constituencies. The deal team should approach negotiations collaboratively and constructively with the Ad Hoc Group and its advisors while firmly maintaining the red lines outlined in Section III of this memorandum. Any proposed deviation from the framework set forth in this memorandum must be approved by Partner Vasquez and, for red line items, by the Company\'s board of directors through General Counsel Susan K. Pratt and CEO Margaret T. Holloway.
410	
411	This memorandum is protected by the attorney-client privilege and the work product doctrine. It reflects confidential legal analysis and strategic advice prepared in anticipation of litigation and in connection with the rendering of legal services to Ridgeline Hospitality Group, Inc. This memorandum should not be shared, forwarded, or disclosed to any person or entity outside of the named recipients and the CC recipient listed on the first page, without the prior written consent of Claire E. Vasquez.
412	
413	For any questions or to discuss any aspect of this memorandum, please contact:
414	
415	> Claire E. Vasquez Partner Ashford Pierce LLP 1261 Avenue of the Americas, 38th Floor New York, New York 10020 Direct: (212) 555-8140
416	>
417	> Email: cvasquez@ashfordpierce.com

21	**[SECTION 2: DIP FACILITY SUMMARY]{.underline}**
22	**2.1 Type and Amount**
23	The DIP Facility shall consist of a senior secured superpriority debtor-in-possession term loan credit facility in an aggregate principal amount of One Hundred Seventy-Five Million Dollars (\$175,000,000) (the \"DIP Facility\"), consisting entirely of new money commitments by the DIP Lenders. The DIP Facility shall be made available to the Borrowers on the terms and subject to the conditions set forth herein and in the definitive DIP credit documentation. The DIP Facility shall not include any revolving credit sub-facility or letter of credit sub-facility.
24	**2.2 Purpose.** Proceeds of the DIP Facility shall be used solely for the following purposes: (a) funding working capital needs and general corporate purposes of the Debtors during the pendency of the Chapter 11 Cases, in each case consistent with the DIP Budget (as defined in Section 7.1 below); (b) payment of costs of administration of the Chapter 11 Cases, including professional fees and expenses of retained professionals of the Debtors and any statutory committee, in each case subject to the Carveout (as defined in Section 9.1 below) and any applicable orders of the Bankruptcy Court; (c) adequate protection payments to pre-petition secured lenders as may be approved by the Bankruptcy Court in accordance with the DIP Orders (as defined below); and (d) such other purposes as may be expressly approved by the Bankruptcy Court and are consistent with the DIP Budget and the DIP Orders (as defined below, the \"Interim DIP Order\" and the \"Final DIP Order,\" and together, the \"DIP Orders\").
25	**2.3 Availability / Draws**
26	The DIP Facility shall be available to the Borrowers in two draws, as follows:
27	> \(a\) **Initial Draw (Interim Draw):** An initial draw of up to One Hundred Million Dollars (\$100,000,000) (the \"Interim Draw\"), which shall be available upon the satisfaction of the conditions precedent set forth in Section 11.1 and the entry of the Interim DIP Order by the Bankruptcy Court.
28	>
29	> \(b\) **Final Draw:** A final draw of up to Seventy-Five Million Dollars (\$75,000,000) (the \"Final Draw\"), which shall be available upon the satisfaction of the conditions precedent set forth in Section 11.2 and the entry of the Final DIP Order by the Bankruptcy Court.
30	Amounts borrowed under the DIP Facility and subsequently repaid or prepaid may not be reborrowed. The two-draw structure provides the Borrowers with immediate access to \$100,000,000 in liquidity upon interim approval by the Bankruptcy Court, with the remaining \$75,000,000 becoming available following final approval.
31	**[SECTION 3: PRICING AND FEES]{.underline}**
32	**3.1 Interest Rate**
33	Interest on the outstanding principal amount of the DIP Facility shall accrue at a rate per annum equal to the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (\"SOFR\") plus 650 basis points (the \"Applicable Rate\"), and shall be payable monthly in arrears in cash on the first business day of each calendar month and on the Maturity Date (as defined in Section 6.1).
34	For purposes hereof, \"SOFR\" shall mean the Secured Overnight Financing Rate as administered by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York (or any successor administrator), with a term commensurate with the applicable interest period (or, at the election of the DIP Agent, such other benchmark as the parties may agree in the definitive documentation), subject in all events to a SOFR floor of 1.00% per annum. In the event that SOFR is unavailable or discontinued, a replacement benchmark shall be determined in accordance with the procedures set forth in the definitive DIP credit documentation, consistent with market conventions then in effect.
35	**Default Rate:** Upon the occurrence and during the continuance of an Event of Default (as defined in Section 15.1), the Applicable Rate shall automatically increase by an additional 200 basis points per annum (i.e., interest shall accrue at SOFR plus 850 basis points per annum during an Event of Default). The Default Rate shall apply to all outstanding DIP obligations, including any overdue interest, fees, and other amounts.
36	Interest shall be computed on the basis of the actual number of days elapsed in a 360-day year.
37	**3.2 Fees.** The following fees shall be payable in connection with the DIP Facility:
38	> \(a\) **Commitment Fee:** A commitment fee of 1.00% per annum shall accrue on each DIP Lender\'s unfunded commitment under the DIP Facility, payable monthly in arrears in cash from the Closing Date (as defined in the definitive DIP credit documentation) until the earlier of (i) the date of funding of such commitment or (ii) the date of termination of such commitment. For the avoidance of doubt, given the two-draw structure and the anticipated six-month term of the DIP Facility, the commitment fee shall apply only to the \$75,000,000 unfunded Final Draw commitment from the Closing Date until such amount is drawn or the commitment terminates.
39	>
40	> \(b\) **Administrative Agent Fee:** An annual administrative agent fee in an amount as separately agreed between the Borrowers and the DIP Agent, payable on the Closing Date and on each anniversary thereof (or, if earlier, on the Maturity Date), in each case pro rata for any partial year.
41	>
42	> \(c\) **Upfront Fee:** None. No upfront fee, closing fee, or funding fee shall be payable in connection with the DIP Facility.
43	>
44	> \(d\) **Exit Fee:** None. No exit fee, prepayment premium, or back-end fee shall be payable in connection with the repayment, prepayment, or refinancing of the DIP Facility.
45	**3.3 Original Issue Discount**
46	None. The DIP Facility shall be funded at par, being 100% of the aggregate principal amount of each draw.
47	**[SECTION 4: ROLL-UP PROVISION]{.underline}**
48	**4.1 Roll-Up Amount**
49	Upon entry of the Final DIP Order, Seventy-Five Million Dollars (\$75,000,000) in aggregate principal amount of pre-petition first lien term loan claims held by the DIP Lenders (the \"Rolled-Up Claims\") shall be \"rolled up\" into the DIP Facility and accorded the same superpriority administrative expense claim status, security interests, liens, and priority as the new money DIP loans. The Rolled-Up Claims shall be allocated among the DIP Lenders pro rata based on their respective commitments under the DIP Facility, such that each DIP Lender\'s portion of the Rolled-Up Claims shall bear the same proportion to the total \$75,000,000 as such DIP Lender\'s DIP commitment bears to the total \$175,000,000 DIP Facility. The roll-up shall be subject to Bankruptcy Court approval as part of the Final DIP Order.
50	**4.2 Roll-Up Mechanics**
51	The Rolled-Up Claims shall be deemed satisfied, discharged, and converted into DIP obligations upon the effectiveness of the roll-up. Each DIP Lender\'s corresponding pre-petition first lien term loan claims shall be reduced dollar-for-dollar by the amount of such DIP Lender\'s share of the Rolled-Up Claims, and such amounts shall instead constitute obligations under the DIP Facility for all purposes. For the avoidance of doubt, after giving effect to the roll-up upon entry of the Final DIP Order, the aggregate outstanding DIP obligations shall equal Two Hundred Fifty Million Dollars (\$250,000,000), consisting of (a) \$175,000,000 in new money DIP loans and (b) \$75,000,000 in Rolled-Up Claims. The Rolled-Up Claims shall bear interest at the Applicable Rate set forth in Section 3.1 from and after the effective date of the roll-up, and all other terms applicable to the new money DIP loans shall apply equally to the Rolled-Up Claims.
52	**4.3 Roll-Up into Exit Facility**
53	Upon emergence from Chapter 11 and the substantial consummation of the plan of reorganization contemplated by the RSA (the \"Plan\"), Seventy-Five Million Dollars (\$75,000,000) of the DIP Facility obligations (equal to the amount of the Rolled-Up Claims) shall be converted into, and shall constitute a portion of, the new first lien exit term loan facility (the \"Exit Term Loan\") contemplated by the RSA. The conversion shall occur on a dollar-for-dollar basis without any additional consideration. The remaining One Hundred Seventy-Five Million Dollars (\$175,000,000) of DIP obligations (representing the new money portion of the DIP Facility) shall be repaid in full in cash from available sources upon the effective date of the Plan. For reference, the total Exit Term Loan contemplated under the Plan is approximately \$595,000,000 (representing 50% of the \$1,190,000,000 face amount of the pre-petition first lien term loans), of which \$75,000,000 would be attributable to the DIP roll-up conversion and the remainder would be funded through other sources as described in the Plan.
